proposals.name: Harlok Yix
proposals.entry:
Known As: The Shambles Butcher, Old Yix, the Orlanian
Home: Patchcoat, the Shambles
Origin: Orlania
Occupation: Veteran, gambler, hired blade, murderer
Status: Notorious and very much at large

“Yix doesn’t cheat at cards. That’s the frightening part.”

Harlok Yix is quite possibly the worst murderer presently walking free in the Shambles.

This is not an official distinction. The Civic Order does not keep useful statistics on such things in the Shambles.

Harlok is an enormous, gray-skinned Orlanian veteran of the Hundred Kingdom Wars, tattooed from scalp to knuckle in the old military and devotional patterns of his vanished homeland. He served through some of the ugliest campaigns of the war and survived the destruction of Orlania by Trovus.

Whatever sort of man went to war did not come home.

There was no home.

Today Harlok lives in Patchcoat, occupying several rooms knocked together above an abandoned dyer’s shop. He drinks, gambles, occasionally works as hired muscle, and murders people with sufficient regularity that his appearances have become part of the neighborhood’s weather.

People know him.

People move when he walks down the street.

And nobody with authority particularly cares.

The Orlanian

Harlok’s immense size makes him memorable, but his tattoos make him unmistakable.

His body is covered in blue-black Orlanian designs: regimental marks, family patterns, victories, mourning spirals, old gods, names, wagers, and symbols whose meanings died along with the people who could read them.

Some are beautiful.

Some have been crossed out.

A few were added after Orlania fell.

Harlok refuses to explain those.

His great lower tusks are an Orlanian trait, yellowed and chipped from age and violence. One bears a narrow brass repair where it was cracked during the war.

He still owns portions of his old campaign armor, particularly a massive spiked shoulder piece that has been repaired so many times that little of the original metal remains.

Harlok has never stopped dressing like a soldier who expects someone to attack before supper.

The Game

Harlok gambles compulsively.

Cards. Dice. Beetle races. Knife pitching. Rat fights. Numbers written on folded scraps of paper. Which tram arrives first. Whether the rain begins before the bell.

He will wager on almost anything.

Strangely, Harlok is not known to cheat.

He despises cheating.

What Harlok cannot endure is losing.

Usually he becomes very quiet.

He studies the table.

He asks whether everyone is certain the game was fair.

Then something terrible may happen.

Not every loss ends in murder. That uncertainty is part of what makes gambling with Harlok so dreadful.

Sometimes he laughs and buys everyone another drink.

Sometimes he leaves.

Sometimes somebody is found behind a boiler house the following morning.

And occasionally Harlok kills the winner before they have even collected the pot.

Among Shambles gamblers there is an expression:

“Don’t win twice from Yix.”

Nobody seems certain whether losing twice is safer.

Veteran of the Hundred Kingdoms

Harlok is not merely a large thug.

He is a trained and extremely experienced soldier.

During the Hundred Kingdom Wars he fought infantry campaigns across several kingdoms before returning to the defense of Orlania during the Trovian invasion.

Harlok understands formation fighting, fortifications, ambushes, artillery, military signals, field medicine, and the thousand ugly practicalities of keeping men alive long enough to kill other men.

He can identify old military equipment almost instantly.

He remembers officers who are now generals.

He recognizes uniforms everyone else has forgotten.

Most dangerously, Harlok does not fight like an angry tavern brute.

He fights like a veteran.

He uses doors, furniture, walls, crowds, mud, stairs and frightened bystanders as weapons. He knows when to advance and when to retreat.

His enormous knife is essentially a short sword in anyone else’s hands.

Patchcoat

Harlok has lived in Patchcoat long enough to become part of its mythology.

Children dare one another to touch his door.

Taverns quietly announce when Yix has arrived so regulars can decide whether to leave.

Bookmakers sometimes refuse his wagers.

Others consider accepting them a badge of courage.

There are people in Patchcoat who genuinely like him.

Harlok occasionally pays someone’s rent.

He once spent three nights digging survivors from a collapsed tenement.

He has carried wounded strangers to doctors.

He gives sweets to children.

Then he murders somebody over dice.

This has made him much harder for Patchcoat to understand than an ordinary monster.

Why Nobody Stops Him

Harlok has been arrested.

Several times.

Charges disappear.

Witnesses reconsider.

Constables discover that jurisdiction is complicated.

Files are misplaced.

More importantly, the Civic Order has little appetite for spending money, officers, or political attention policing murders among the poor of the Shambles.

When violence threatens respectable districts, Civic Vigilance suddenly becomes remarkably efficient.

Patchcoat receives paperwork.

Harlok understands this perfectly.

He rarely kills outside the Shambles.

Fate

High Concept: Last War-Dog of Dead Orlania

Trouble: Fortune May Take My Coin, But Never My Pride

Harlok can accept bad luck.

What he cannot accept is the humiliation of being beaten.

Every lost wager becomes personal. Every victorious opponent becomes, for one dangerous moment, an enemy who has taken something from him.

Aspect: I Survived What Killed My Country

Harlok has endured bombardment, starvation, sieges, disease and the destruction of Orlania. Threatening him is difficult because almost nothing in Fogport compares to things he has already seen.

Aspect: Everybody in Patchcoat Knows Yix

His reputation opens doors, empties rooms and silences witnesses. Unfortunately, being famous also means that almost everyone knows where to find him.

Aspect: A Soldier Notices the Battlefield

Harlok instinctively reads exits, cover, weapons, weak structures and frightened people. A tavern becomes terrain the moment trouble begins.

Aspect: There Are Still Some Things I Will Not Do

Nobody is entirely certain what those things are.

Neither is Harlok.

posts.name: Gamemaster Only
posts.entry:
Harlok Should Not Begin as a Boss Fight

Harlok works best if Byl and Lott meet him first as a problem they cannot neatly categorize.

He may even be useful.

The interesting question is not simply whether they can defeat Harlok.

It is what they do when a terrible man becomes useful to them.

Possible First Encounter — The Empty Chair

Byl and Lott need information from a gambling room in Patchcoat.

There is one empty chair.

Someone warns Byl not to sit there.

Naturally, circumstances eventually put him there.

The chair belongs to Harlok Yix.

Harlok arrives.

Rather than immediately becoming violent, he becomes amused by Byl and insists that the magician play one hand with him.

The stakes should initially be trivial.

Then Harlok recognizes something about Byl, Lott, or an object they are carrying.

The game suddenly matters.

Lott and Harlok

Harlok should find Lott fascinating.

Most people look at Lott and see a brute.

Harlok sees immediately that Lott is dangerous.

He respects that.

He may repeatedly attempt to communicate with Lott in the strange shorthand of veteran fighters: pointing out exits, commenting on weapons, offering him food, silently moving a chair capable of supporting his weight.

This creates an uncomfortable possibility:

Harlok likes Lott.

Lott may even like Harlok before discovering exactly what he has done.

That is considerably more interesting than having them immediately punch each other.

Byl and the Cards

Harlok eventually learns that Byl carries cards.

This should become dangerous.

He wants Byl to play.

Not because Byl is famous.

Because Harlok suspects that a magician can influence chance.

If Byl beats him, Harlok becomes obsessed with discovering whether magic was involved.

If Byl loses, Harlok may become delighted with him.

If Byl obviously cheats, Harlok becomes terrifyingly calm.

The Orlanian Connection

Harlok possesses knowledge from the Hundred Kingdom Wars that almost nobody in Fogport has.

This gives him recurring usefulness.

He might recognize:

  • a Trovian military cipher;
  • an old Orlanian weapon;
  • a retired war criminal living under another name;
  • a symbol appearing somewhere beneath Fogport;
  • a former officer now employed by the Civic Order;
  • military cargo that absolutely should not exist anymore.

His memories should occasionally turn what appears to be an ordinary Fogport mystery into unfinished business from the war.

The Murder He Didn’t Commit

Eventually someone is murdered in Patchcoat in unmistakable Harlok fashion.

Everyone assumes Yix did it.

Harlok insists he didn’t.

Almost nobody believes him.

The Civic Order is delighted to discover an opportunity to close several unsolved murders simultaneously by hanging Harlok for all of them.

Unfortunately for Byl and Lott, Harlok really is innocent of this particular murder.

Proving that means saving a murderer from execution.

Harlok considers this hilarious.

Someone Is Protecting Him

The Civic Order’s indifference explains much of Harlok’s freedom.

It may not explain all of it.

Someone occasionally removes particularly troublesome reports concerning Harlok.

Possible reasons:

Harlok knows what happened during a classified campaign late in the Hundred Kingdom Wars.

Someone in Fogport fought beside him.

Someone owes him.

Or somebody has been keeping the old Orlanian alive because they expect to need him again.

Harlok himself may not know which.

The Thing He Will Not Do

Harlok’s final Aspect should eventually become important.

Despite everything he has become, there remains a boundary left over from the man he once was.

Perhaps he will not harm children.

Perhaps he will never abandon someone who served beside him.

Perhaps he refuses to kill a surrendered enemy.

Perhaps he cannot tolerate Trovian atrocities being repeated in front of him.

Do not establish the answer immediately.

Let Byl and Lott discover it through play.

Finding the last surviving piece of Harlok Yix’s decency should make him more complicated, not redeem him.

He is still the worst murderer in the Shambles.
